title: Corporate catering for banks and finance firms: a complete guide
body_markdown:
Banks and finance firms’ corporate catering is food and service planned around workplace meetings, client hospitality and business events, with the aim of feeding guests without disrupting the agenda. Corporate catering for banks and finance firms needs a clear brief: who can enter the building, where food can be served, when service must stop and who approves changes.


**TL;DR**

- Corporate catering for banks and finance firms should follow the meeting agenda, building access rules and dietary brief.
- myCHEF suits Dubai businesses seeking corporate catering with menus and practical arrangements agreed for their event.
- Choose boxed meals for individual distribution, buffets for staggered breaks and plated service for seated hospitality.
- Compare written inclusions, staffing, equipment and clearance responsibilities before approving a catering proposal.


For a tailored proposal, [contact myCHEF](https://www.mychef.ae/contact) with your event details and ask which catering format fits the venue and agenda. This guide explains how to prepare that brief and compare the responses, rather than rank caterers.

## Why catering needs a different brief in finance

A board meeting, an internal training session and an investor reception need different service arrangements. Start with the purpose of the gathering, not a menu shared from a previous event.

For a confidential meeting, keep catering activity outside the room while discussions are underway. For a reception, give guests somewhere to place glasses and plates without crowding registration. For training, arrange food around the actual break rather than an assumed lunchtime.

**The right format protects the meeting’s purpose.** A carefully chosen menu still falls short if delivery interrupts a presentation or guests spend their break waiting to be served.

In a Dubai office tower, ask facilities management about loading access, visitor registration, service lifts and the route to the meeting floor. Treat these as venue-specific questions, not arrangements the caterer can assume.

## How do you plan catering for a bank or finance firm?

### Define the event and its service boundaries

Start with a shared document or email. Record the event purpose, audience, room and agenda, then separate essential requirements from preferences. A working lunch needs food people can manage beside meeting materials; a client dinner needs a different conversation about table service and pacing.

Identify the person authorised to approve the menu and the person responsible for the venue. Give the caterer one consolidated brief rather than separate requests from reception, facilities and the executive assistant.

For confidential sessions, agree where the catering team can wait and when someone will invite them into the room. Do not include sensitive meeting content in a document circulated to suppliers.

- State whether the event is internal, client-facing or open to invited guests.
- Provide the agenda and identify the permitted service breaks.
- Name the event approver and the on-site contact.
- Mark rooms and corridors that suppliers must not enter.
- Define the final service and collection times.

### Match the format to the room and agenda

Sketch the room layout before requesting menus. Mark entrances, seating, presentation equipment and the proposed food station. A buffet needs a practical route for guests; a plated meal needs access around the tables.

Use the comparison below to shortlist a format. If delegates must remain seated throughout a presentation, do not plan a buffet that requires everyone to leave their place. If attendance is staggered, ask how service will work across those arrivals.

myCHEF provides corporate event catering in Dubai. When requesting a proposal, ask which formats the team can deliver for your setting; do not assume that a particular staffing arrangement or equipment package is included.

- Choose individual meals when distribution matters more than table service.
- Consider a buffet when guests can leave their seats during a break.
- Discuss plated service for a seated hospitality event.
- Reserve a separate surface for drinks and used tableware.
- Check that the proposed layout leaves doors and working routes clear.

### Build the menu around how guests will eat

Collect dietary requirements directly through an appropriate internal channel. Ask about allergies separately from preferences, and share only the information the catering team needs to prepare and identify meals.

**Do not treat a dietary label as a complete allergy assessment.** Ask the caterer about ingredients, preparation and cross-contact controls for each declared allergy. Confirm the proposed arrangement with the affected guest rather than making assurances on the supplier’s behalf.

An illustrative working-lunch brief might request a chicken main, a vegetarian main, rice or another accompaniment, separately dressed salad and individual desserts. This is a planning example, not a myCHEF package or a menu confirmed for booking.

- Ask guests to distinguish allergies from preferences.
- Specify any halal, vegetarian or vegan requirements.
- Request clear identification of dietary meals.
- Discuss sauces, dressings and serving utensils.
- Agree who hands a separately prepared meal to its intended guest.

### Confirm access, equipment and staffing

Walk the route from the building entrance to the service area with your facilities contact. Check what is actually available: a pantry does not establish that cooking, reheating or washing up can take place there.

Share the practical findings with the caterer. Ask what will arrive ready to serve, what requires preparation on site and what equipment needs to be brought in. Confirm any venue permissions before accepting a proposed cooking setup.

For staffing, define the tasks rather than requesting an unspecified team. Delivery, setup, replenishment, table service, clearing and final collection are separate responsibilities. **The person who delivers the food is not automatically responsible for managing the room.**

- Confirm supplier entry procedures and delivery access with the building.
- Describe the preparation area and available facilities accurately.
- List tables, crockery, cutlery and other equipment needed.
- Assign responsibility for replenishment and used tableware.
- Confirm where staff can wait and store equipment.
- Agree waste handling and the collection route.

### Compare proposals using the same written scope

A shared spreadsheet is enough to compare proposals. Use the same headings for each caterer so that a shorter proposal does not appear simpler merely because it leaves responsibilities unstated.

Menu choices, guest count, service format, staffing, equipment and access arrangements all belong in the discussion. Ask each supplier to explain how changes to those requirements affect the quotation. Keep payment terms, amendment terms and cancellation terms alongside the event scope for approval.

When reviewing a myCHEF corporate catering proposal, check the written inclusions rather than assuming serving staff, drinks, tableware or cleaning are part of the request. A tailored service still needs a precise agreement.

- Compare the menu and the quantity basis used for each dish.
- Check staffing roles and the agreed service period.
- Separate equipment supplied from equipment supplied by your venue.
- Record exclusions and responsibilities retained by your team.
- Confirm approval, amendment and cancellation terms in writing.

### Create the handover and contingency plan

Before the event, bring the approved menu, floor plan, access instructions and contacts into one operational brief. Use clear version control so that an old guest count does not remain in circulation after an amendment.

Decide who can authorise changes on the day. If the meeting runs late, the catering team needs an instruction from a named contact—not conflicting requests from several guests. Ask the caterer how a delayed service would be handled before it happens.

For recurring office events, record what worked and what needs changing. Keep feedback practical: distribution, portion suitability, labelling, room layout and clearance are more useful than a general rating.

- Reconfirm the agreed attendance and dietary requirements.
- Share the final room layout and arrival instructions.
- Name the person authorised to change service timing.
- Agree how delays and attendance changes will be communicated.
- Confirm the final clearance and equipment collection arrangements.

## Which catering format fits your event?

Choose the service format before refining individual dishes. The table compares operational options, not confirmed myCHEF packages; ask the caterer which arrangements suit your venue.

| Option | Best for | Practical advantage | Key limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Individual boxed meals | Training sessions and working lunches | Each guest receives a separate meal | Distribution and packaging clearance still need an owner |
| Buffet service | Team gatherings with a shared break | Guests choose from the agreed dishes | Requires serving space and a workable queue route |
| Plated service | Seated client hospitality and formal dinners | Guests remain seated during service | Needs coordinated staffing, table access and pacing |
| Canapé service | Networking receptions and standing events | Food can circulate while guests talk | Requires a clear brief on whether it replaces a meal |

A mixed format can work, but it adds decisions. For example, a reception followed by a seated meal needs separate timings, service arrangements and equipment checks. Do not add formats simply to make the event feel more elaborate.


![Four catering formats: individual boxed meals, buffet service, plated service and canapé service](https://media.get-ryze.ai/workspace-article-images-public/e263eb14-5ba0-46fc-b3f2-1baf666a6aa4/body-036db41848c66264501e1c53eefac856.jpg)

*Choose the format around seating, available space and the meeting agenda.*


## What should the catering proposal include?

A useful proposal connects the menu to the work required to serve it. Ask for dish descriptions, the agreed attendance, dietary arrangements, service timings and the division of responsibilities between your office and the supplier.

The main scope decisions are practical. Cooking on site introduces equipment and venue questions. Table service introduces staffing and pacing questions. A longer event introduces questions about replenishment, drinks and clearance throughout the programme.

Check exclusions with equal care. Ask whether the proposal covers table linen, glassware, serving equipment, beverages, ice, setup, clearing and collection. These are questions to resolve, not standard inclusions to assume.

For procurement approval, retain the accepted proposal and any subsequent amendments together. Your event organiser, facilities contact and catering contact should be working from the same final scope.

## Common mistakes banks and finance firms should avoid

### Scheduling service during confidential discussions

A scheduled delivery time is not permission to enter a meeting room. Agree a holding location and a signal from the organiser before food or staff move into the space. Keep confidential papers away from the service area.

### Leaving reception to solve supplier access

Reception needs instructions, not an unexpected delivery to manage. Confirm the supplier contact, entry route and receiving person with the building team in advance. Check whether the proposed arrival falls within permitted access arrangements.

### Choosing food before checking the furniture

A menu that needs knives, generous plate space and repeated clearing is a poor match for a room arranged around laptops and documents. Review the room layout and eating arrangements before approving dishes.

### Collecting dietary information without a handover

A list of requirements is not enough if nobody knows which guest receives which meal. Agree identification and distribution with the catering team. Keep personal details limited to what is necessary for that task.

### Comparing quotations with different responsibilities

A delivery-only proposal and a staffed event proposal describe different work. Compare like-for-like responsibilities before approval, especially setup, service, equipment and clearance. Otherwise, your office inherits tasks it has not planned to cover.

## FAQ


**What is the best catering format for a bank board meeting?**

Choose a format that fits the board meeting’s agenda and confidentiality requirements. Individual meals suit straightforward distribution, while plated service requires planned access and staffing; agree when the room can be entered.

**Can a finance firm arrange catering without an office kitchen?**

Brief the caterer on the facilities available and ask for a menu and service plan that fits them. Confirm preparation, holding, serving equipment and collection arrangements before approving the proposal.

**What should we send when requesting corporate catering in Dubai?**

Send the date, location, guest count, event purpose, service format and agenda. Include dietary requirements, building access instructions and the details of the person approving the event.

**Is drop-off catering enough for a client event?**

Drop-off catering fits a client event only when your team can manage the remaining service tasks. Assign setup, distribution, replenishment and clearance explicitly; otherwise, discuss a staffed arrangement.

**How should banks handle catering for guests with allergies?**

Collect allergy information separately from food preferences and discuss each requirement with the caterer. Confirm ingredients, cross-contact controls and meal identification without promising that a dietary label guarantees suitability.

**What affects a corporate catering quotation?**

The menu, guest count, service format, staffing, equipment and practical venue arrangements shape the quotation. Compare written inclusions and exclusions, and request an updated proposal when the event scope changes.

**Does myCHEF provide catering for corporate events?**

myCHEF provides corporate event catering in Dubai. Send the event brief and ask the team to confirm the menu, service format, staffing and practical arrangements appropriate to your venue.

## Set the clearance time before approving the menu

The meeting is not finished when the food arrives. Decide when used plates, packaging and equipment must leave the room, particularly if another meeting follows. That final handover belongs in the brief from the start.

For a tailored myCHEF proposal, send your **date, Dubai location, guest count and service required**. Include the agenda, dietary requirements and any building-access restrictions so the discussion starts with the arrangements your event actually needs.
